Poisson spike-train deconvolution

Source: vignettes/articles/deconvolution.Rmd
deconvolution.Rmd

In deconvolution, a design matrix contains shifted copies of a point-spread function. Sparse coefficients represent sharp events, while the measured signal is blurred and noisy. For nonnegative Poisson intensities,

Y_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}\{(X\beta)_i\},\qquad\beta\geq0.

The following examples each have 10,000 observations, 10,000 candidate peak locations and 1,000 true peaks. L0glm fits the Poisson likelihood directly; the native OpenMP backend shares the sparse convolution design across channels.

Single channel deconvolution 

library(L0glm)
single <- simul(method=2L, n=10000L, p=10000L,
  n_nonzero=1000L, seed=2L)
comparison <- sparseglm(single, family=poisson("identity"),
  method=c("L0glm", "lasso", "relaxed_lasso"),
  tune="gic", nlambda=10L, nonnegative=TRUE, intercept=FALSE,
  approximation="wls", lambda=list(L0glm=log(10000)*log(log(10000))),
  options=list(L0glm=list(relaxed=TRUE)))
L0glm.metrics(comparison)[c("method", "seconds", "gic", "TP", "FP", "FN", "TN",
  "F1_score", "MCC")]
Method Seconds GIC TP FP FN TN F1 MCC
L0glm 0.22 102682 845 154 155 8846 0.845 0.828
LASSO 0.40 145904 950 2096 50 6904 0.470 0.467
Relaxed LASSO 0.64 122083 905 999 95 8001 0.623 0.607

The observed and true signal are shown above zero; fitted signals and estimated spikes are mirrored below in red. The panels compare L0glm with the strongest competing method in this example, ranked by support MCC.

The coefficient comparison shows estimation accuracy and the additional coefficients selected by the competing method. Each common (0,0) is plotted once.

plot(comparison, which=c(1L, 3L))

Multichannel deconvolution

Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC/MS) provides a natural application: compounds with overlapping chromatographic peaks contribute counts across many mass-to-charge channels. Peak locations are shared across channels, while each compound has its own sparse mass spectrum. A grouped Poisson model recovers the peak locations and the corresponding spectra together.

The simulation retains all 226 informative mass channels generated from the spectral library. No channels are discarded for fitting or plotting.

multi <- simul(method=4L, n=10000L, p=10000L,
  n_nonzero=1000L, seed=2L)
comparison_multi <- sparseglm(multi, family=poisson("identity"),
  method=c("L0glm", "lasso", "relaxed_lasso"),
  tune="gic", nlambda=10L, nonnegative=TRUE, intercept=FALSE,
  approximation="wls_grouped",
  lambda=list(L0glm=log(10000)*log(log(10000))),
  options=list(L0glm=list(relaxed=TRUE, ncores=8L)))
L0glm.metrics(comparison_multi)[c("method", "seconds", "gic", "TP", "FP", "FN", "TN",
  "F1_score", "MCC", "within_row_F1_score", "within_row_MCC")]
Method Seconds GIC TP FP FN TN F1 MCC Within-row F1 Within-row MCC
L0glm 34.14 5615963 944 11 56 8989 0.966 0.962 0.909 0.864
Group LASSO 244.87 7413616 980 860 20 8140 0.690 0.685 0.842 0.768
Relaxed group LASSO 906.34 6138687 909 309 91 8691 0.820 0.802 0.853 0.782

Row F1 and MCC measure recovery of peak times. Within-row F1 and MCC measure mass-spectrum sparsity among correctly recovered true-positive peaks. Group LASSO and relaxed group LASSO use glmnet’s grouped Gaussian approximation, with shared row weights 1/(rowMeans(y)+0.1); every model is evaluated using the original Poisson likelihood and the same GIC. Each glmnet path has ten lambda values. Relaxed group LASSO refits the selected shared row support with gamma=0.

Correlated peaks and group LASSO

Shifted copies of the point-spread function are strongly correlated. For this design, the standard group-LASSO irrepresentability diagnostic is 20.54, well above the bound of one. This helps explain why group LASSO can retain many neighbouring peak locations even while reconstructing the observed signal well. L0glm’s direct support penalty gives a much cleaner separation of the peaks.

To compute the diagnostic, let A be the shared-row-weighted design with columns scaled to unit norm, S the true row support and U_{j\cdot}=B^*_{j\cdot}/\|B^*_{j\cdot}\|_2. We evaluate

\max_{j\notin S}\left\| A_j^\top A_S(A_S^\top A_S)^{-1}U_S \right\|_2.

The standard group-LASSO selection conditions require this quantity to be at most one, with a strict inequality giving a sufficient condition under the assumptions in Bach (2008). This diagnostic concerns the unconstrained weighted-Gaussian group model; the benchmark additionally uses nonnegativity constraints and Poisson scoring. The diagnostic script gives the calculation and numerical solve check.

Compare the recovered signals and spectra

Heatmaps stack the observed data, ground-truth coefficients and selected methods on one page. Coefficient panels share a colour scale; observed counts have their own intensity scale. Cyan overlays mark true support or true positives, red marks false positives and magenta marks false negatives. Legends also give the counts. Every channel is retained.

plot(comparison_multi, type="heatmap", which=c(1L, 3L))
plot(comparison_multi, type="coefs", which=1:3, channels="all")

Multichannel true-versus-estimated coefficient panels use a single column. Blue points are correctly recovered nonzero coefficients, red points are false positives and magenta points are false negatives.

Tune or use native validation 

gic <- L0glm.tune(multi$X, multi$y, family=poisson("identity"),
  tune="gic", nlambda=10L, nonnegative=TRUE, grouped=TRUE, relaxed=TRUE)
cv <- L0glm.tune(multi$X, multi$y, family=poisson("identity"),
  tune="cv", nfolds=5L, nlambda=10L, nonnegative=TRUE, grouped=TRUE, relaxed=TRUE)

For held-out checkpoint stopping, supply validation=list(X=V, y=v). OpenMP remains available through the native backend. See the validation example and the full benchmark tables.

The L0 deconvolution idea was inspired by work by de Rooi & Eilers (2011). Our methods for automatically setting regularization, the extensions to Poisson or negative-binomial noise, and the multichannel shared-support extensions are new developments of the present work. simul() supports all three noise models.
